text: Probably the pressure to succeed early. Young people compare themselves with others online all the time, and it seems as if everyone else already has a great job, a car and perfect holidays. Exams and the cost of housing add to that. I think the pressure isn't necessarily greater than in the past, but it's more visible and harder to escape.

questions.question: What causes the most stress for young people today?

text: Yes, because stressed employees make more mistakes and leave more often, so it's in the company's own interest. Simple steps can make a big difference: realistic deadlines, not sending messages late at night, and managers who actually ask how people are doing. Some companies offer gym memberships or quiet rooms, which is nice, but it can't replace a reasonable workload.

questions.question: Should employers do more to reduce stress at work?

text: For some people, being busy has become part of their identity, so resting makes them feel guilty or lazy. Others simply never switch off, because their phone keeps work and news with them all the time. I'd suggest starting small — twenty minutes a day of something with no purpose other than enjoyment, like a walk without headphones.

text: For some people they're a useful starting point, because they make meditation feel less mysterious and give clear instructions. I tried one for a month and noticed I fell asleep faster. The irony, though, is that you're using a phone to escape from stress that often comes from phones. In the long run, I think habits like sport or walking are more reliable.

questions.question: Are apps for meditation and relaxation actually helpful?

text: Not really, in my experience. By the second week you finally relax, and then you go back and the stress returns within days. Shorter breaks more often, for example a long weekend every couple of months, seem to work better. Even more important is having time to rest every evening, because a holiday can't fix a routine that's exhausting the rest of the year.
